In a within-subject validation study (N = 51), CaliGaze was evaluated against a Tobii Pro Spark infrared eye tracker while participants completed a risky binary choice task with simultaneous dual-system recording.

To ensure high data quality, we implemented a predefined exclusion criterion: any participant with more than 100 trials (out of 147 per condition) showing substantial data loss or failing to capture gaze within our regions of interest (ROIs) would be excluded.
All participants provided written informed consent and received performance-contingent compensation (see Incentive Structure for details).
Participants were seated at a distance of approximately 65 cm from the screen.
On each trial, participants were presented with two simultaneously displayed options: a risky option and a safe option.

table.text: Instead, the preregistered target of 30-40 valid participants was set pragmatically on the basis of the sample-size range commonly used in laboratory studies of this type, rather than on a formal power calculation. We initially recruited 52 participants from Shanghai International Studies University. To ensure high data quality, we implemented a predefined exclusion criterion: any participant with more than 100 trials (out of 147 per condition) showing substantial data loss or failing to capture gaze within our regions of interest (ROIs) would be excluded. One participant met this criterion because of Tobii data loss and was excluded from all cross-device and modeling analyses, resulting in a final analytic sample of N ¿ 51 (M_age ¿ 22.49 years, SD = 2.32; 32 female participants). For descriptive purposes, a sensitivity analysis conducted in G*Power 3.1.9.7 (Faul et al., 2007) indicated that, with N ¿ 51, α ¿ 0.05, and 80% power, the minimum detectable effect for a two-tailed within-subject paired comparison was Cohen's dz ¿ 0.40. This calculation contextualizes only the paired mean-comparison design and does not constitute a power analysis for the correlation, agreement, or hierarchical modeling analyses. It was not used to determine recruitment. The research protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Shanghai International Studies University (Approval No. 2026BC007). All participants provided written informed consent and received performance-contingent compensation (see Incentive Structure for details).

To ensure high data quality, we implemented a predefined exclusion criterion: any participant with more than 100 trials (out of 147 per condition) showing substantial data loss or failing to capture gaze within our regions of interest (ROIs) would be excluded.
All participants provided written informed consent and received performance-contingent compensation (see Incentive Structure for details).

On each trial, participants were presented with two simultaneously displayed options: a risky option and a safe option.

Second, participants completed a mandatory rest break between blocks to reduce cognitive fatigue and maintain stable task engagement throughout the session.

If the participant had chosen the safe option on the sampled trial, they received the guaranteed amount c ; if the participant had chosen the risky option, the actual outcome was determined by a computerized random draw based on the stated probabilities ( x 1 with probability p, and x 2 with probability 1 -p).

text.text: Eye-tracking has become central to process-tracing research in judgment and decision-making, yet access to this paradigm remains constrained by the cost and logistical demands of researchgrade infrared systems.

We present CaliGaze, an open-source webcam eye-tracking framework that uses geometric iris landmark estimation, individually calibrated piecewise spatial mapping, and a recorded single-eye eyelid-opening validity flag to support ROI-level gaze classification in binary choice experiments.

In a within-subject validation study (N = 51), CaliGaze was evaluated against a Tobii Pro Spark infrared eye tracker while participants completed a risky binary choice task with simultaneous dual-system recording.
CaliGaze showed strong cross-device agreement in ROI-level dwell proportions and reproduced the core fixation-choice signatures of the task.

Both gaze streams consistently supported gaze-dependent over gaze-independent evidence accumulation, and attentional-weighting estimates showed strong cross-device correspondence in between-participant rank ordering.

These results suggest that CaliGaze can support ROI-level process tracing and gaze-dependent computational modeling in binary choice tasks, offering a scalable and accessible alternative for decision researchers, with particular potential for largescale, remote, or resource-limited settings.

Eye-tracking technology has emerged as a fundamental tool in the behavioral sciences, providing an empirical window into the latent cognitive processes that govern decision behavior and information acquisition (Orquin & Mueller Loose, 2013; Wedel & Pieters, 2008).

CaliGaze combines four implementation components: (1) a within-eye-width-normalized iris-position ratio (ρ) that reduces sensitivity to uniform changes in facial scale (Lu et al., 2014); (2) median-based piecewise mapping for participant-specific task-specific calibration (Guestrin & Eizenman, 2006); (3) a recorded singleeye eyelid-opening validity flag for identifying samples potentially affected by eyelid closure (Cech & Soukupova, 2016); and (4) sequential webcam acquisition and processing within the Pygame stimulus loop, with host-clock timestamps used for post hoc alignment with the asynchronous Tobii callback.

text.text: Because CaliGaze uses standard RGB video and anatomical landmark geometry rather than infrared corneal reflections, it is not affected by cornealreflection-specific mechanisms in the same way as infrared systems.

This difference may reduce some failure modes, but it does not eliminate participant-or condition-specific data-quality problems: spectacle glare, optical occlusion, illumination, camera placement, and landmark loss may still increase calibration error or missing data.
Eligibility and data-quality decisions should therefore be based on observed calibration and tracking performance rather than categorical assumptions about participant groups.

By integrating these features, CaliGaze provides an accessible framework, validated here against a Tobii Pro Spark in a value-based binary choice task, for ROI-level process tracing and gaze-informed computational modeling.

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study.
The cross-device correlation analyses and the classic singleparameter attentional drift diffusion model (aDDM0) were specified in the preregistration and were completed as planned.

The ICC and Bland-Altman agreement analyses, the asymmetric aDDM1 and aDDM2 specifications, and the comparisons among the DDM and aDDM variants were developed after data collection and are therefore treated as exploratory.

The final implementation differed from the preregistered plan in two design-related respects: both eyetracking systems were recorded simultaneously on every trial rather than in counterbalanced blocks, permitting direct trial-by-trial comparison, and the final sample (N ¿ 51) exceeded the preregistered target of 30-40 valid participants.
The preregistered aDDM0 was retained and is fully reported in Supplementary Appendix S7; aDDM1 and aDDM2 were evaluated as exploratory extensions rather than replacements for the preregistered model.

No formal a priori power analysis was used to determine the sample size.

Instead, the preregistered target of 30-40 valid participants was set pragmatically on the basis of the sample-size range commonly used in laboratory studies of this type, rather than on a formal power calculation.
We initially recruited 52 participants from Shanghai International Studies University.

To ensure high data quality, we implemented a predefined exclusion criterion: any participant with more than 100 trials (out of 147 per condition) showing substantial data loss or failing to capture gaze within our regions of interest (ROIs) would be excluded.

One participant met this criterion because of Tobii data loss and was excluded from all cross-device and modeling analyses, resulting in a final analytic sample of N ¿ 51 (M_age ¿ 22.49 years, SD = 2.32; 32 female participants).

To evaluate low-cost gaze tracking, we implemented a dual-system recording setup in which a Tobii Pro Spark served as the high-precision hardware reference and CaliGaze served as the webcam-based validation system.
Both systems recorded during the same decision task, enabling trial-by-trial comparisons.
They were not hardware-synchronized: CaliGaze was sampled sequentially within the Pygame loop, whereas Tobii supplied samples asynchronously through its SDK callback.
Trial phase labels and host-clock timestamps supported post hoc alignment within the unified stimulus-presentation program.
Both acquisition streams and the behavioral log recorded host time using Python time.time().

For CaliGaze, the host timestamp was written after camera capture, Face Mesh inference, smoothing, screen mapping, and ROI assignment; the Tobii callback stored a host time.time() value together with the device and Tobii system timestamps.
Behavioral variables such as show_start and show_end also used time.time().

Because show_start was recorded before the decision display was drawn and flipped, and record_mp_frame() was called before pygame.display.flip(), these values are software event or logging times rather than direct measurements of physical display onset or camera exposure.
They support post hoc trial-and phase-level alignment but not sub-frame synchronization.

Gaze data were recorded using a Tobii Pro Spark remote infrared eye tracker (Tobii Technology AB, Stockholm, Sweden) sampling at 60 Hz.
The device was attached to the lower bezel of a 16.1-inch laptop screen (1920 × 1080 resolution).
Participants were seated at a distance of approximately 65 cm from the screen.

Each 147-trial context began with a nine-point calibration, and calibration was repeated after each 49-trial segment.

text.text: The experimental procedure was programmed and administered using the Pygame library.
Participants performed a computerized binary choice task designed to assess risk-taking behavior across 294 trials, divided into two conditions based on reward magnitude (0, 40 vs.
On each trial, participants were presented with two simultaneously displayed options: a risky option and a safe option.

To minimize potential spatial-response biases, the left/right positions of the risky and safe options were independently randomized on each trial, so that fixations toward a given location reflected attention to that option's value rather than a fixed spatial or motorresponse tendency.

The risky option offered a predetermined probability ( p) of obtaining a higher monetary reward ( x 1 ) and a complementary probability (1 -p) of a lower reward ( x 2 ), such that its expected value was defined as EV risk = p ⋅ x 1 +(1 -p )⋅ x 2 .
In contrast, the safe option provided a guaranteed monetary amount (c) with 100% certainty (EV safe = c).
By systematically manipulating the parameters p , x 1 , x 2 and c, the task generated a broad distribution of expected-value differences ( Δ EV=EV risk -EV safe ).

This parametric design was specifically intended to introduce a range of "easy" trials (large Δ EV) and "difficult" trials (Δ EV near zero), allowing for a robust estimation of individual-specific psychometric choice curves.
To ensure that decisions reflected genuine subjective preferences, participants were explicitly instructed that there were no objectively "correct" responses.

The task was also incentive-compatible: at the conclusion of the experiment, one trial was randomly selected and paid out according to the participant's actual choice, with the resulting earnings added to a fixed participation payment.
This procedure was intended to maintain task engagement and encourage truthful valuation throughout the experiment.
The complete instruction materials are provided in Supplementary Appendix S8.

To examine whether absolute stake magnitude shapes both risk preference and visual attention, the experiment employed a within-subjects design featuring two distinct reward-magnitude conditions administered within a single session: Across both conditions, risky gambles were constructed using seven probability levels ( p ∈ {5 % , 10 % , 25 % , 50 % , 75 % , 90 % , 95 % }), while safe-option values varied in fixed 2 RMB increments across the corresponding payoff range.

The two conditions were matched on both the distributions of expected value differences ( Δ EV ) and the proportion of trials in which the risky versus safe option had the objectively higher expected value.

This matching procedure ensured that any observed differences in choice behavior, gaze allocation, or computational-model parameters could be attributed specifically to changes in absolute stake magnitude rather than to confounding differences in task difficulty or choice structure.
Several procedural controls were additionally implemented to ensure data quality and internal validity.
First, block order was counterbalanced across participants (i.e., half completed the Low-Magnitude block first) to mitigate potential order, carryover, and fatigue effects.
Second, participants completed a mandatory rest break between blocks to reduce cognitive fatigue and maintain stable task engagement throughout the session.
The task was entirely self-paced, with no response time limit, ensuring that the full gaze sequence underlying each choice was captured without truncation by time pressure.
As illustrated in Fig. 3, each trial followed a standardized temporal sequence consisting of fixation, decision, and response-confirmation phases.

text.text: At the beginning of each trial, a central fixation cross (" +¿ ") was displayed for a jittered duration of 800 -1000 ms to orient participant's gaze and establish a neutral attentional baseline.
Subsequently, the risky and safe options appeared simultaneously on the left and right sides of the screen (positions randomized).
Participants indicated their choice by pressing the " f " key (left-hand option) or the " j " key (right-hand option).

Immediately following a response, a red border appeared around the selected option for a jittered interval of 600 -800 ms, providing explicit visual confirmation of the participant's choice before the onset of the subsequent trial.
Monetary outcomes were not revealed during the task but deferred until the final payment phase, minimizing possible learning, wealth effects, or sequential dependencies across trials.
The experiment employed an incentive-compatible payment scheme to ensure that participants' choices reflected genuine risk preferences rather than satisficing or random responding.
All participants received a fixed attendance fee of 50 RMB regardless of their choices.
In addition, a performance-contingent bonus was determined using the Random Lottery Incentive System (RLIS; Holt & Laury, 2002).
text.formatted: In addition, a performance-contingent bonus was determined using the Random Lottery Incentive System (RLIS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Holt & Laury, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Upon completion of the 294 experimental trials, the computer randomly selected one trial to be played out for real payment.

If the participant had chosen the safe option on the sampled trial, they received the guaranteed amount c ; if the participant had chosen the risky option, the actual outcome was determined by a computerized random draw based on the stated probabilities ( x 1 with probability p, and x 2 with probability 1 -p).
The bonus payment ranged from 0 to 60 RMB, making total compensation meaningfully contingent on participants' revealed choices.
Total payment (the fixed fee plus the realized bonus) was transferred to the participant via WeChat Pay or Alipay immediately after the session.

To transform raw gaze coordinates into discrete gaze events for computational decision modeling, the gaze time series from each system were processed according to their respective hardware and sampling capabilities.
For the Tobii Pro Spark, raw 60 Hz gaze coordinates were processed offline using a velocity-threshold identification (I-VT) algorithm (Salvucci & Goldberg, 2000) under default configurations.

text.text: Gaze samples with a point-to-point velocity below 30°/s were categorized as fixations, temporally adjacent fixations separated by saccadic intervals shorter than 75 ms were merged, and fixations shorter than 60 ms were excluded.
For CaliGaze, up to K = 5 of the most recently appended iris-position-ratio values were averaged once online before piecewise screen mapping and ROI assignment.
During the first K -1 appended samples, the mean used all values currently in the buffer; thereafter it used the most recent K values.
Values with Valid = 0 were still appended, whereas camera or landmark-detection failures produced no appended value.
At the observed median intersample interval of 32.0 ms, a full K = 5 window spanned approximately 128 ms from its first to last sample and had a nominal group delay of approximately 64 ms.
No second moving-average stage was applied.

Because the lower and variable sampling rate of standard webcams precludes reliable velocity-based parsing, consecutive temporally adjacent CaliGaze samples assigned to the same target ROI were aggregated into ROI dwells (fixation-like ROI dwell episodes), rather than oculomotor fixations.
Processed gaze events were mapped to the left and right target regions.
The two option rectangles each covered 30% of screen width and 40% of screen height.
Tobii used its measured two-dimensional gaze point for point-in-rectangle classification.

CaliGaze mapped only the xcoordinate and fixed y = H/2 for collision testing against the same rectangles; because H/2 lay within both rectangles, CaliGaze classification was effectively determined by their left-right boundaries.
LEFT and RIGHT labels were translated post hoc into risky and safe identities using the randomized trial-specific layout for subsequent validation, behavioral, and aDDM analyses.

To quantify subjective value differences between the risky and safe options at the trial level, we estimated the subjective value of the risky option using each participant's certainty equivalent (CE).
The CE represents the guaranteed amount at which a participant is indifferent between a risky gamble and a safe outcome and thus serves as a behavioral estimate of subjective value.

Although choices in the experiment were collected through randomized binary decisions rather than explicit price lists, the payoff structure allowed participants' revealed preferences to be reconstructed as an implicit price list for each probability level and magnitude condition.

Specifically, for each participant, magnitude condition, and probability level, the risky option was paired across trials with a series of safe amounts spanning the full payoff range in fixed increments.
These safe amounts were then sorted in ascending order to reconstruct an ordered preference sequence.
Participants' choices across the reconstructed sequence were used to infer the CE.

When a participant switched from choosing the risky option to choosing the safe option between two adjacent safe amounts, the CE was estimated as the midpoint between these values, following standard multiple price-list procedures (Holt & Laury, 2002; Andersen et al., 2006).
text.formatted: When a participant switched from choosing the risky option to choosing the safe option between two adjacent safe amounts, the CE was estimated as the midpoint between these values, following standard multiple price-list procedures <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Holt & Laury, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Andersen et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: In cases involving non-monotonic choice patterns with multiple switching points, an implied switching position was inferred based on the total number of risky choices, yielding a unique CE estimate.

Similar approaches to handling inconsistent switching behavior in multiple price-list paradigms have been discussed in prior work (e.g., Jacobson & Petrie, 2009; Andreoni & Sprenger, 2012; Engel & Kirchkamp, 2019; Chew et al., 2022).

To establish an empirical foundation prior to computational modeling, we conducted a series of model-independent analyses to characterize choice behavior under risk, validate gaze measurement across devices, and examine the relationship between attentional allocation and choice behavior.

We first examined behavioral regularities using standard descriptive indices, including overall risky-choice proportion, sensitivity to objective risk probability, subjective value difference (derived from certainty equivalents), and response time as a function of decision difficulty.
We next characterized attentional allocation during decision-making using deviceappropriate gaze episodes, operationalized as Tobii fixations and CaliGaze ROI dwells.

The extracted metrics were: (1) risky dwell proportion, defined as the proportion of total optiondirected episode duration allocated to the risky option; (2) the identity and duration of the first option-directed episode; and (3) the identity and duration of the last option-directed episode before response.
Risky dwell proportion served as the primary index of attentional allocation, the principal cross-device validation metric, and the attentional input for the subsequent aDDM analyses.
To validate the reliability of webcam-based gaze estimation, we assessed the consistency of risky dwell proportion between Tobii and CaliGaze at the group, individual, and trial levels.
The cross-device correlation analyses were preregistered; the ICC and Bland-Altman analyses were exploratory assessments of absolute agreement and systematic bias.
We then examined whether gaze allocation was associated with choice behavior before fitting the computational models.

These exploratory signatures included the duration of first, middle, and last gaze episodes, associations of the first and last episodes with subsequent choice, and shifts in psychometric choice functions conditional on episode identity (Krajbich & Rangel, 2011).

text.text: Binary outcomes were coded 1 for the focal response and 0 otherwise: risky versus safe choice, selection versus nonselection of the first-fixated option, and selection versus nonselection of the lastfixated option.
Objective probability was divided by 100; fixation duration was analyzed in seconds; subjective-value differences were analyzed in the original task-value units.
Continuous predictors were not mean-centered or z-standardized.
Trial-level binary outcomes were estimated with binomial mixed-effects logistic regression using a logit link, Wald 95% confidence intervals, and two-sided Wald z tests.
Response time was estimated with a linear mixed-effects model using Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.
Each mixed model included a participant-specific random intercept only; no random slopes were fitted.

The behavioral models pooled the two stake-magnitude conditions and included one applicable fixed predictor: objective probability, subjective-value difference, or absolute subjective-value difference.
Device-specific fixation-choice models were fitted separately for Tobii and CaliGaze.
The final fixation-choice model included additive fixed effects of subjective-value difference and last-fixation identity (safe fixation as the reference level), without an interaction.
Exact model formulas, singular-fit diagnostics, and analytic sample sizes are reported in Supplementary Appendix S5.

To quantify cross-device agreement in average risky dwell proportion at the participant level between Tobii and CaliGaze, we used paired-samples t-tests, Pearson correlation, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), and Bland-Altman analyses.
Analyses were conducted separately for each magnitude condition.

Paired-samples t-tests were used to assess mean differences between devices, Pearson correlations were used to assess whether individual differences were preserved across devices, whereas ICCs and Bland-Altman analyses were used to evaluate absolute agreement.
Absolute agreement was quantified using two-way mixed-effects, single-measure intraclass correlation coefficients for absolute agreement, ICC(A,1).
This specification is appropriate for assessing agreement between measurements obtained from individual devices rather than averages across devices.
ICC estimates were reported with 95% confidence intervals.

Following commonly used interpretation guidelines, ICC values below 0.50 were considered poor, values between 0.50 and 0.75 moderate, values between 0.75 and 0.90 good, and values above 0.90 excellent (Koo & Li, 2016).

text.text: Bland-Altman analyses were conducted to characterize systematic bias and limits of agreement between devices.
For each participant and condition, the difference score was calculated as CaliGaze minus Tobii, and the mean of the two device measurements was used as the reference magnitude.
Mean bias was defined as the average device difference, and 95% limits of agreement were calculated as the mean bias ± 1.96 times the standard deviation of the difference scores.

Proportional bias was assessed by regressing the device difference scores on the paired-measurement means; a significant slope indicated that cross-device disagreement varied as a function of measurement magnitude.
These analyses followed standard recommendations for Bland-Altman method-comparison studies (Bland & Altman, 1986; Giavarina, 2015; Gerke, 2020).

text.text: To further characterize the cognitive mechanisms underlying value-based decision-making, we implemented a gaze-independent drift diffusion model (DDM) and three variants of a gazedependent attentional drift diffusion model (aDDM0, aDDM1, aDDM2).

The gaze-independent DDM provides a baseline account in which choices are determined solely by value differences, whereas the aDDM extends this framework by incorporating gaze allocation as a dynamic modulator of evidence accumulation.
All models used the same behavioral variables, whereas the aDDM variants were fitted separately using trial-level gaze measures derived from Tobii and CaliGaze.
Behavioral data were merged with device-specific trial-level fixation summaries.

Trials without any fixation classified within either target ROI for a given device could not contribute to the dwell-proportion predictors and were therefore omitted from that devicespecific aDDM dataset.
Of the 14,994 behavioral trials from 51 participants, 32 Tobii trials and 24 CaliGaze trials lacked usable left-or right-ROI fixation data.
The response-time criterion of RT > 0.2s removed no additional trials after this merge.

text.text: Consequently, 14,962 Tobii trials (0.21% excluded) and 14,970 CaliGaze trials (0.16% excluded) were retained for modeling.

Following prior applications of drift diffusion modeling in value-based and social decisionmaking (Chen & Krajbich, 2018; Chen et al., 2023), we implemented a biased DDM to characterize individual risky-choice behavior.

To examine whether visual attention was associated with trial-level modulation of evidence accumulation during risky decision-making, we implemented a regression-based attentional driftdiffusion model (aDDM) that extends the standard DDM by incorporating gaze-conditioned value weighting into the mean drift rate.
In this implementation, gaze entered through trial-level dwell proportions rather than a fixation-by-fixation generative process.

The relative contribution of each option to evidence accumulation could therefore vary with the distribution of gaze within a trial, such that attended and unattended information contributed differently to decision formation.

This formulation builds on prior work showing that visual attention can influence value-based choice by modulating the integration of attended versus unattended information (Cavanagh et al., 2014; Sheng et al., 2020 Sheng et al., , 2023)).

For a given trial i, the mean drift rate was defined as: v i ~Gaze risk ,i * ( β risk ,GazeRisk * U risk ,i -β s afe ,GazeRisk * U s afe ,i ) +Gaze s afe ,i * ( β risk ,GazeS afe * U risk ,i -β s afe ,GazeS afe * U s afe ,i ) where Gaze risk ,i and Gaze s afe ,i denote the proportions of fixation durations within the two options' ROIs allocated to the risky and safe options, respectively, and U risk and U s afe denote the expected values of the risky and safe options.

The coefficients β risk ,GazeRisk , β s afe ,GazeRisk quantify the contributions of the currently attended risky and safe values, whereas β risk ,GazeS afe , and β s afe ,GazeS afe characterize the corresponding unattended-value contributions.
Because the safevalue terms enter the drift equation with a minus sign, a larger safe-value weight shifts evidence accumulation toward the lower safe-choice boundary.

The first model (aDDM0) corresponded to the original attentional drift diffusion model proposed by Krajbich et al. (2010).

text.text: Within the regression-based implementation, coefficients associated with attended information were constrained to be identical across option types ( β risk ,GazeRisk =β safe ,GazeSafe ), and coefficients associated with unattended information were likewise constrained to be identical ( β risk ,GazeSafe =β safe ,GazeRisk ).

Under these constraints, attentional modulation was characterized by a single attentional-weighting parameter, corresponding to the relative weighting of unattended versus attended value information irrespective of whether the option was risky or safe.
The second model (aDDM1) followed the coefficient-based implementation proposed by Sheng et al. (2020) and allowed all four gaze-dependent value-weighting coefficients to be freely estimated.
text.formatted: The second model (aDDM1) followed the coefficient-based implementation proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Sheng et al. (2020)</ref> and allowed all four gaze-dependent value-weighting coefficients to be freely estimated.

text.text: Consequently, attentional modulation could vary independently as a function of both gaze state and option type.
The model also estimated starting point (z), boundary separation (a), and non-decision time (t) analogously to the baseline DDM.

The third model (aDDM2) imposed a symmetry constraint on the coefficients associated with attended value information while allowing unattended value coefficients to differ between risky and safe alternatives.

Specifically, the model assumed that the value coefficient associated with the currently fixated option was identical regardless of whether the attended option was risky or safe: β risk ,GazeRisk =β safe ,GazeSafe .

Under this formulation, attentional weighting of unattended information remained asymmetric across risky and safe alternatives, thereby reducing model complexity relative to the fully unconstrained aDDM1 while preserving the key asymmetry of theoretical interest.

Together, these models span different degrees of flexibility in attentional value weighting: a single attentional-discounting parameter (aDDM0), a fully unconstrained formulation (aDDM1), and an intermediate constrained formulation (aDDM2).

Model comparison was evaluated using multiple complementary criteria rather than a single fit index.

The primary criterion for model selection was the Widely Applicable Information Criterion (WAIC; Watanabe, 2010), which estimates out-of-sample predictive performance while accounting for effective model complexity through integration over the full posterior distribution.
Following the implementation in dockerHDDM, WAIC values were reported on the deviance scale (-2 × ELPD), with lower values indicating superior predictive performance.
Relative model performance was evaluated using pairwise differences in WAIC ( Δ WAIC), with larger differences indicating stronger evidence favoring one model over another.

Posterior predictive checks (PPCs) evaluated whether the fitted models reproduced key features of the observed choice and response-time data.
Trial-level predictions were generated conditional on posterior parameter draws and the observed trial covariates.

Model predictions were compared with the observed overall response-time distribution, participant-level mean response times, overall risky-choice proportion, participant-level risky-choice proportions, and the binned relationship between risky dwell proportion and risky-choice probability.
For each model, 100 posterior draws were sampled without replacement using a fixed random seed (2026).

For each draw, 20 signed response times were simulated per observed trial from the Wiener first-passage-time (WFPT) density implemented in HDDM; the sign identified the simulated boundary choice and the absolute value represented response time.
Predictions were summarized across posterior draws and repetitions and visually compared with the corresponding empirical patterns.
These checks were used to assess absolute model adequacy and complemented the relative model-comparison indices.

We first compared the baseline DDM with the three attentional models (aDDM0, aDDM1, and aDDM2) to evaluate whether incorporating gaze allocation improved model performance.

The original single-parameter attentional model (aDDM0), corresponding to the classic formulation proposed by Krajbich et al. (2010), failed to improve upon the baseline DDM and yielded substantially poorer fit according to both WAIC and DIC in the Tobii and CaliGaze datasets.

(2010)</ref>, failed to improve upon the baseline DDM and yielded substantially poorer fit according to both WAIC and DIC in the Tobii and CaliGaze datasets.

text.text: This finding suggests that a single attentional-weighting parameter was insufficient to capture the attentional dynamics underlying risky decision-making in the present task.
Detailed results for aDDM0 are reported in Supplementary Appendix S7.
In contrast, both asymmetric attentional models (aDDM1 and aDDM2), which allowed attentional discounting to vary across option types, substantially outperformed the baseline DDM.
Across both datasets, these models yielded markedly lower WAIC and DIC values, indicating improved predictive performance when gaze-dependent modulation of evidence accumulation was incorporated.
These findings indicate that risky decision-making was better characterized by asymmetric attentional influences than by value-based accumulation alone.
We further compared two variants of the aDDM that differed in their parameterization of gaze-dependent effects.
The information criteria did not converge on a single ranking: WAIC favored the constrained variant (aDDM2) across both datasets, whereas DIC favored the fully flexible variant (aDDM1).

The two variants nonetheless produced broadly comparable posterior predictive patterns, and the more flexible aDDM1 showed lower sampling efficiency (smaller effective sample sizes and higher R ] values).

Accordingly, subsequent parameter analyses in the main text focus on the more parsimonious constrained variant (aDDM2), based on comparable empirical adequacy, greater parsimony, and more stable estimation rather than unanimous support across information criteria; results from the fully flexible specification (aDDM1), together with the classic single-parameter aDDM specified in our preregistration, are reported in Supplementary Appendix S7.

text.text: Across both datasets, the posterior mean of the shared coefficient for currently fixated option values was larger than the posterior means of both unattended-value coefficients, consistent with the core assumptions of the attentional drift diffusion framework.

For example, in the Tobii dataset, the estimated coefficient associated with attended option values was 0.061, whereas the unattended-value coefficients were smaller, with greater attenuation for the unattended risky value than for the unattended safe value ( β risk , gazesafe = 0.006; β safe , gazerisk = 0.043).

A similar pattern was observed in the CaliGaze dataset, in which the attended-value coefficient (0.056) exceeded the unattended-value coefficients ( β risk , gazesafe = 0.016; β safe , gazerisk = 0.048).
Under the fitted model, this coefficient pattern indicates gaze-dependent value weighting, with currently fixated values receiving larger estimated weights than unattended values.

To facilitate interpretation relative to the classic aDDM framework, we additionally derived attentional weighting indices reflecting the relative contribution of unattended information during evidence accumulation.
Across both datasets, the group-level estimates of both θ risk and θ safe were below 1, indicating reduced weighting of unattended option values relative to attended information at the group level.
However, θ risk was markedly smaller than θ safe in both datasets (Tobii: 0.107 vs.
0.713; CaliGaze: 0.280 vs.
0.854), indicating that unattended risky information was more strongly attenuated than unattended safe information during evidence accumulation.
This asymmetry indicates that safe-option value continued to shape evidence accumulation even when it was not fixated, whereas risky-option value exerted its influence primarily while attended.
Thus, safe-option value was comparatively gaze-invariant, whereas risky-option value was more attention-dependent during risky decision-making.

The present study evaluated CaliGaze, a webcam computer vision framework, by benchmarking it against research-grade infrared eye tracking during a within-subject binary choice task.
CaliGaze successfully reproduced established signatures linking fixation to choice.

Across both gaze streams, attentional DDMs (aDDMs) outperformed the standard DDM that is independent of gaze, and CaliGaze closely matched Tobii on core decision parameters while preserving differences between participants in attentional weighting.
Together, these findings demonstrate that gaze tracking via webcams can support process tracing with the aDDM, providing a more accessible approach to study the role of attention in decision-making.
The central finding of this evaluation is the substantial consistency observed between CaliGaze and the Tobii infrared reference system across multiple levels of analysis.

text.text: CaliGaze's accessibility contribution lies not in replacing infrared eye tracking across all applications, but in lowering the entry barrier for paradigms that require reliable ROI-level classification in spatially separated displays rather than fine-grained gaze localization in two dimensions.
Its use of commodity RGB cameras and open-source software reduces dependence on specialized hardware, dedicated laboratory infrastructure, and proprietary acquisition systems.

This portable and transparent measurement pipeline may be particularly valuable for laboratories with limited resources, multisite projects, and replications of decision paradigms that incorporate gaze data on a larger scale.
In this sense, CaliGaze shifts the primary implementation challenge from hardware acquisition to calibration specific to the task and data quality control.
Several limitations define the scope of the present findings.
First, CaliGaze was evaluated in a spatially separated binary-choice paradigm, for which its within-eye-width-normalized iris-position ratio was specifically optimized.

Extending the framework to vertically distributed or multi-alternative displays, including 2 × 2 choice arrays and reading tasks, will require improved two-dimensional gaze mapping and task-specific validation.
Second, the present validation used a fixed laboratory setup with controlled lighting and an external webcam.

Although CaliGaze's modular architecture supports browser-based deployment, its performance across heterogeneous cameras, lighting conditions, viewing distances, postures, and computing environments remains to be established.

The present sample also consisted of university students from a single institution; validation in more demographically and clinically diverse populations would help establish the broader generalizability of the framework.

Third, the two devices showed close agreement for the core decision parameters and preserved individual differences in attentional weighting, but the absolute scale of the attentional weighting estimates differed across devices, particularly for θ safe .
These parameters are therefore better suited to within-device comparisons and rank-order analyses than to direct comparison of absolute values across devices.
Finally, the associations between parameters and choices were estimated from the same choices used to fit the models and therefore should not be interpreted as independent predictive validation.
Future work should examine out-of-sample prediction, test-retest reliability, and parameter recovery using simulation and independent data.

Choice and response time were jointly modeled using four core parameters: drift rate (v), starting point (z), boundary separation (a), and non-decision time (t).
The drift rate reflects the direction and speed of evidence accumulation; positive drift favors movement toward the upper boundary, whereas negative drift favors movement toward the lower boundary.
The starting point captures pre-decisional bias before evidence accumulation begins.
Boundary separation reflects decision caution, and non-decision time accounts for perceptual and motor processes.

The drift rate ( v ) was modeled as a linear function of the expected values of the risky and safe options: v = β risk * U risk + β s afe * U s afe where U risk and U s afe denote the expected values of the risky and safe options, respectively.
The coefficients β risk and β s afe represent the weights assigned to the two options during evidence accumulation.

Under the present response coding, a larger positive β risk increases drift toward the upper risky-choice boundary, whereas a larger magnitude of the negative coefficient | β safe | increases drift toward the lower safe-choice boundary.

To characterize the relative influence of the risky option on evidence accumulation, we additionally computed a risk-option weighting index defined as the ratio β risk /| β safe | , with larger values indicating greater relative weighting of the risky option during the decision process.
